prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology and active forms of glucagon-like peptide-1 that made incretin-based therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity possible

statement.case_for: GLP-1 is the most complete arc from hormone physiology to medicine on the shortlist: proglucagon processing, identification of the active GLP-1(7-36) forms, demonstration of insulinotropic action in humans, and then drugs with large, independently confirmed effects on glycaemia, weight and cardiovascular and renal outcomes. Five of six members placed it first, but I weigh it on the science: the discovery is original, mechanistically clear, replicated by many groups and has had lasting impact. A discovery-oriented trio of Drucker, Holst and Mojsov rewards the physiology and the identification of the active peptide, which is the kind of contribution the prize has traditionally honoured.
statement.case_against: The credit boundary is the weak point. Knudsen's long-acting acylated analogue is what made the medicine real, so a discovery-only trio can be read as leaving out the person without whom patients would not benefit. Others outside the supplied credit list (for example Habener, by my recollection, not verified here) also contributed to the original peptide work. If the committee wants a prize that spans discovery and therapy, any three of four names will leave out someone with a legitimate claim.

responses.point: Linnarsson ranks GLP-1 first but credits Drucker, Holst and Knudsen, treating long-acting analogue development as part of the discovery-to-drug chain, and leaves Mojsov out.
responses.response: I take the point that the prize should reflect a transformative medicine, but I disagree on the third name. Knudsen's work is major drug engineering, whereas Mojsov identified and characterised the active peptide on which every downstream step depends. For a prize about physiology and medicine, I would keep the third place for the discovery of the active hormone. I accept that this is a judgement call and that Knudsen's claim is stronger than that of most development-stage candidates on our list, so I would not call the choice clear-cut.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius also ranks GLP-1 first with Knudsen as the third laureate, and places TOR (Hall and Schreiber) second as a foundational concept with broad consequences.
responses.response: We agree on the first place and differ on attribution. On TOR I am more reserved: Hall's identification of TOR is clearly decisive, but pairing him with Schreiber leaves out the mammalian mTOR work, and Sabatini's contribution is not secondary. That makes the TOR configuration harder to defend than GLP-1, where the discovery chain is better delimited. I would keep TOR as a serious candidate for a later year rather than this one.

responses.point: Sandberg places the unfolded protein response (Walter and Mori) first as a new mode of organelle-to-nucleus signalling, with GLP-1 second.
responses.response: I agree that the UPR is a clean, conceptually original, two-person discovery with very good attribution, and it is my fallback if the committee judges the GLP-1 attribution too contested. Where I disagree is on ranking it above GLP-1: its link to Physiology or Medicine is still mostly through mechanism, with clinical translation developing, whereas the GLP-1 work has already changed medicine at scale. I would put UPR first only if our attribution debate on GLP-1 cannot be resolved.

responses.point: The chair ranks GLP-1 first with Drucker, Holst and Mojsov, and places optogenetics second while noting it is a classic more-than-three attribution problem.
responses.response: I agree with the GLP-1 trio. On optogenetics I share the chair's concern: Deisseroth, Nagel and Hegemann leaves out Boyden, Bamberg and Miesenböck, and I do not think an allocation that excludes them would be easy to defend. As a neuroscientist I recognise the method's impact on circuit research, but I do not let that familiarity carry weight in ranking it; it is a tool whose clinical reach is still early, and the credit problem is real.

uncertainties: Whether the committee prefers the physiology-and-discovery trio (Drucker, Holst, Mojsov) or one that includes Knudsen for the drug development.
Whether researchers outside the supplied credit list have priority claims on the original peptide work; this cannot be resolved from the shortlist.
Whether the optogenetics attribution problem (six credited names) can be resolved in any three-person configuration.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the shortlisted candidates. I co-authored a 2009 paper with Thomas Perlmann, a fellow committee member, on stem-cell-derived dopamine neurons, which is not related to any shortlisted ballot. I will disclose any link that emerges, for example on optogenetics, where I work in a neighbouring field but have no documented involvement.
